text: Two soldiers, tired of soldiering, decide the shortest route out of the ranks is to find a country without a king and take the job. Kafiristan is remote enough that nobody will check their credentials. Much of what follows is logistics - how to cross the mountains, how to drill men who speak another language, how a rifle becomes an argument - and Peachy Carnehan talks through most of it, because the whole venture is a story being told at speed. Then the people there decide Danny Dravot is a god, and the improvisation acquires a congregation. The Academy gave the film its costume prize, which is nearer the point than it sounds: everything here depends on what a man appears to be at fifty paces. Huston takes 129 minutes and never hurries them.

The condition is a year apart before marriage may be mentioned again, and the film takes the entire year seriously. Claude meets Ann in Paris early in the century, is invited to her family's house in England, is intended for her sister, and attaches himself to Muriel instead. Separation of that length is conducted on paper, and Truffaut lets the correspondence set the tempo: two households, two languages, weeks between a question and its answer. He is French, they are English, and in that decade the Channel is enough to make any feeling unverifiable. What the film keeps returning to is how much of a love affair is administered by other people - mothers, calendars, the post. 130 minutes for a courtship conducted at a distance, and the delay is never an obstacle to the story. The delay is the story.

Seventy-three minutes, two people, one walk: a son takes his mother, who is dying, out into open country. That is the whole premise, which leaves the image, the weather and the quiet to carry everything else. A German production spoken in Russian, set nowhere that requires a name. Everything depends on duration: the walk takes as long as walking takes. Sokurov gives the son's tenderness a practical shape - the lifting, the carrying, the finding of shade - so that care looks like work, because it is. The patience the film asks for is specific: a hillside held long enough to stop being scenery. Grief is never announced. It is simply the condition the afternoon takes place in, and the film does not lighten as it goes.

A studio musical from 1941 that keeps interrupting itself to point out that it is a studio musical. Olsen and Johnson, stage comedians with a hit to convert, spend the picture arguing with the picture: the frame is addressed, the projection is addressed, and the plot about two young people in love is handled as an obligation to be discharged between gags. Eighty-four minutes, with a joke rate set by men who learned timing in front of audiences that were free to walk out. What survives best is the disrespect for continuity - a running gag can outlive the scene that produced it, and the romance is never permitted to believe it is the reason anyone bought a ticket. It sits on the TSPDT thousand, a strange destiny for something built to be thrown away.

A rash is a minor complaint; a visit to the clinic is not, when the patient crossed from Myanmar without papers. The rash goes unexplained, and the film seems content with that. His girlfriend does the talking, and her friend comes along for the errands. Much of the first stretch is exactly that - waiting, arranging, being looked at - filmed at the speed such things actually take. Then the day empties out, the three of them head out of town, and Weerasethakul lets heat and duration do the work that plot usually does. 128 minutes, and no voice is raised in any of them. The pleasure is not a break from the precarity: the same status that makes a doctor's office dangerous is what turns an afternoon of shade and idleness into something earned.

Its maker called it a comedy set in a haunted movie studio, and most of the haunting is done by Hollywood. Forty-two minutes; a crowd of men and women whose genders the film declines to settle, vamping for a camera close enough to be complicit. It opens as a joke - a mock commercial for lipstick that will not come off - and the joke curdles fast into something nearer a nightmare, with an assault at the hinge of it. Jack Smith works in costume-box glamour: veils, lace, the posture of a studio starlet, worn by people no studio would have cast. That it ended up on a thousand-greatest list is the least interesting fact about it. Forty-two minutes is not long to watch. It is a long time to have watched.

To make an instructional film about drinking, the authorities require the two young men who caused the trouble to cause it again, on camera, in the same restaurant, until the take is usable. A prosecutor supervises. A teacher attends. The repetition is the whole engine: one night's stupidity has to be performed to order, and each attempt drains a little more excuse out of it. Pintilie made this in Romania in 1968, which means the joke - a state that would rather stage a lesson than understand an incident - had to be told in a room where someone was listening. The comedy is genuine and it thins by the hour. Romanian critics voted it into their all-time ten four decades later, by which time it had hardened into something other than satire.

In 1916 the front line runs between an officer's uniform and his mother tongue. Apostol Bologa serves the Habsburgs; the men in the trenches opposite are Romanians, which is to say his own, and the war has arranged matters so that doing his job well is a form of treason against himself. Ciulei takes 165 minutes, and the length is not indulgence - the drama is deferral, doubt advancing an inch at a time, in rooms behind the line where nothing is decided. Desertion here is less a decision than a temperature. There is a love story, and it does what love stories do for a man in that position: it stands as evidence that a life outside the uniform remains theoretically available. Romanian critics have kept it in their all-time ten.

Two wandering singers carry a bride away from her own wedding; in the film's other half, a widow works herself past exhaustion trying to keep a sick daughter alive. Eighty-one minutes for both, which leaves no room for explanation, and none is offered. Veroiu builds the two parts from the same rural materials - stone, weather, obligation, a village that watches - and lets them rhyme rather than connect. The mode is closer to ballad than to drama: figures instead of psychologies, gestures repeated until they carry weight, silence where another film would insert a motive. Nothing here suggests the countryside is innocent. Romanian critics have kept it on their all-time ten; it is a hard, short film about love arriving late or not arriving.

Romania, 1957, and the crime on offer is not a robbery but an appetite. The film follows one man's slow conversion by money: the wanting of it, the arranging of a life around it, the small permissions granted early that make the later ones easy. Iliu spends his 110 minutes on the conversion rather than the consequences, which is the harder half to dramatise - there is no single moment when a decent man becomes another thing, only a run of afternoons in which he is a little less able to refuse. It is filed as a crime picture, and the label fits only on the understanding that the offence begins years before anything illegal happens. Romanian critics voted it into their all-time ten in 2008, half a century after it was made.

A television cameraman and the person he is filming end up caught in the same difficulty, which is professional for one of them and private for both. In Romania in 1980 television belonged to the state, and that sits under every frame without being argued. Daneliuc's interest is the ordinary coercion of the job: the way a lens converts a person into material, the way agreement given at the start of a shoot cannot be taken back once the tape exists. 104 minutes of negotiation between people who each hold something the other needs. The work and the private trouble do not run in parallel; they contaminate one another. Romanian critics later placed it in their all-time ten, which for a film about broadcasting is an irony worth having.

The same film crew turns up in all three episodes, and in the first they are doing two jobs at once - the picture the state has commissioned and the one they actually want to make. Tatos builds everything out of that doubleness. In the second, they are scouting a restaurant and the owner, handed a listener, unloads his life across the table at length. In the third, the camera drifts to the background of a shot, where two extras have been seated to eat, and finds that the background is where the century has been kept. 98 minutes, with the joins between the parts left deliberately loose. Romania, 1982: making films nobody believes in is simply part of the working week, and the film is funny about it in the way that being watched is funny.

The prize for exceeding the quota is a boat trip on the Danube, shared with everyone else who exceeded theirs. The river does the moving; hardly anyone else does. Daneliuc puts the organisers and the organised on one deck for 122 minutes and watches the arrangement come apart in small increments: the officials defend the timetable, the young passengers want the night, and nobody can get off. A holiday awarded rather than chosen is a strange thing to be inside, and the film keeps locating the precise points where enjoyment turns into duty - the announcements, the arranged entertainment, the obligation to be seen having a good time. Made in 1981, and it never says a word against the system that booked the trip. The itinerary says it.
